newsitem.title: USA: US housing starts flat in July, seen rising ahead.
newsitem.headline: US housing starts flat in July, seen rising ahead.

text.p: New homebuilding in July was in line or slightly below most estimates, but persisted at solid levels and is seen providing ongoing economic strength in the third quarter, economists said.

Housing starts were unchanged at an annualized 1.447 million-unit rate in July, after June's increase was revised downwards to up 3.2 percent from 4.8 percent. Several economists predicted a 1.5 million-unit peak in coming months.
Building permits grew 1.4 percent to 1.422 million units, after June's drop was pared to 2.1 percent from 2.6 initially.

"Optimism is quite high and there is strong growth in employment and income," said Samuel Kahan, president of A.S.K. Financial Research Ltd. Housing "will not be a source of weakness for the economy at least for the rest of the year."

Mortgage lenders have indicated summer strength in both new home purchases and refinancings. Several mortgage industry analysts have noted that inventories remain moderate, boding well for more new homebuilding.
"There is no real sign of weakness in the housing sector," said Richard Berner, Mellon Bank chief economist. "It's just another source of economic strength" in the third quarter.
Soft spots did appear in some regions in July. But economists generally attributed those declines to weather conditions or other short-lived factors.

Housing starts in the Northeast surged 41.4 percent, the region's fastest growth rate since November 1994. But other areas saw starts decline: 3.7 percent in the Midwest, 2.4 percent in the South and 5.3 percent in the West.

"The data were a tiny bit stronger than they look on the surface," Berner contended. "There were a lot of weather issues we've had to contend with, floods and the like, which have clearly clouded the interpretation of these numbers."
Single-family housing starts increased by 2.7 percent last month, while starts of multi-family units lost 8.9 percent.
"You got a little more bang for the buck out of single-family starts," said Berner. "Nevertheless, we probably haven't seen the full effect on housing from the decline in rates" this summer.

The likely 1.5 million-unit peak, Kahan added, "would be significantly lower than the 2.1 million-unit peak reached in the 1970s or the 1.7 million-unit rate reached a couple of years back." But, he said, "that's not surprising," given various tax law and demographic changes. "In absolute terms, 1.5 million would be a pretty healthy number."
